title: Confirmation's gifts (CCC 1302–1305)
hook: it deepens baptismal grace, strengthens, and sends

segments.voice: Yesterday, baptism and hope: baptism is necessary, yet the Church entrusts to mercy those who never received it. Your line was God is not bound.

A line forms in the center aisle. Teenagers in their best clothes, a few adults, each with a sponsor standing close behind, a hand on the shoulder. At the front, the bishop. One by one they step up. He calls each by the name they've chosen, dips his thumb in oil, traces a cross on the forehead, says a few words about the gift of the Holy Spirit, and wishes them peace. Afterward there are photos and cake. But the Catechism says something was given in that moment, and that it pushes outward.
screen: `A LINE IN THE CENTER AISLE.` → `OIL, A CROSS, A FEW WORDS.` → `WHAT WAS GIVEN?`

segments.voice: Day one hundred twenty-seven met the oil and the seal; today, what they do. The Catechism calls the effect of Confirmation a special outpouring of the Holy Spirit, like the one the apostles received at Pentecost, and it moves in three ways. First, it deepens. Confirmation doesn't replace baptism; it brings baptismal grace to growth. It roots a person more deeply as a child of God, who can call God Father. It unites them more firmly to Christ, and binds them more closely to the Church. It increases the gifts of the Holy Spirit, gifts named from Isaiah's picture of the promised king, in the Douay-Rheims: "the spirit of counsel, and of fortitude." Second, it strengthens: a special strength of the Spirit to spread and defend the faith in word and action, to confess Christ's name boldly, and never to be ashamed of the cross. Third, it sends. Just before the Ascension, in Acts, Jesus tells the apostles they'll receive the power of the Holy Spirit, "and you shall be witnesses unto me." That's the direction of the whole sacrament: out the door. Like baptism, Confirmation is given only once. It leaves an indelible spiritual mark, a seal, a sign that Christ has claimed this person with his Spirit. Quoting Thomas Aquinas, the Catechism says the confirmed receive the power to profess their faith publicly, almost as an official duty. So the oil on the forehead isn't an ending. It's a sending, and the cake is the send-off.
screen: `A SPECIAL OUTPOURING OF THE SPIRIT.` · `IT DEEPENS BAPTISM.` · `IT STRENGTHENS FOR WITNESS.` · `IT SENDS, AND IT SEALS ONCE.` · then, large: `YOU SHALL BE WITNESSES UNTO ME.`

segments.voice: Think of one place where you go quiet about something you care about: a table where you change the subject, a group chat where you don't type what you think, a friend you haven't been honest with. If you pray, ask the Holy Spirit for courage there, in the Church's old words, Come, Holy Spirit, or in silence; if you don't, notice what courage would look like in that one place.
Confirmation's gifts. It deepens the grace of baptism, strengthens a person to witness, and sends them, sealed once and for good. Today's word.
Your line: sent. The cross on the forehead points out the door. Day one thousand ninety-six, done.

howItsDone: In the Latin rite the bishop usually confirms, anointing the forehead with chrism; candidates choose a sponsor and often a saint's name. In the Eastern Catholic churches the sacrament, called chrismation, is given right after baptism.

notes: Confirm Challoner wording of Isaiah 11:2 and Acts 1:8.
Hook describes a typical Latin-rite confirmation (sponsor's hand on the shoulder, chosen name, 'peace be with you'); practices vary. The words of the rite are described, not quoted.
The gifts are named via Isaiah 11:2; the Catechism's list of the gifts (CCC 1831) is not counted, to keep within the claims rule.
'Come, Holy Spirit' offered as an existing prayer line (Veni Sancte Spiritus / Veni Creator), not a new prayer. Confirm.
howItsDone: 'often a saint's name' and the Eastern practice of chrismation right after baptism (CCC 1290–1292) are outside the cited paragraphs; confirm.
Original: Latin 'confirmatio' (plain ASCII by design); ecclesiastical pronunciation. No etymology claimed.

Audit pass: in the Latin rite the bishop says the confirmand's chosen name in the anointing formula; the hook had the candidates saying it themselves (fixed). CCC 1302 speaks of a 'special' outpouring of the Spirit, not a 'full' one (teach, screen head and myth reveal fixed).
